## Structural notes

1. **The result has no number.** "Incidents dropped a lot after the freeze" asks the reader to trust you. "Most of our worst outages started on a Friday" has the same problem. You read the incident log, but the reader gets no figure from it.

Then "Our release tool also batched every deploy" adds a second cause. Say "two reasons", or attach the batching to the first cause. Do not cut the batching: it is a separate idea.

- **"The batching made rollbacks slower."** Safe cut. The clause before it ("could not tell which change had broken production") already shows this.

- The "people who wrote the change go home" sentence.
- The "nine on Saturday" scene.
- Ana's quote.
- The last sentence, "a weekend spent reading someone else's code".

Replace "Incidents dropped a lot" with the before and after counts from the incident log.
artifact.draft.md:
# Why we stopped deploying on Fridays

For two years our team shipped whenever a change was ready, Friday afternoons included. Most of our worst outages started on a Friday. The pattern was hard to miss once we read the incident log.

Friday deploys fail for a dull reason. The people who wrote the change go home, and the people on call over the weekend did not write it. When something breaks at nine on Saturday, the on-call engineer has to read an unfamiliar diff before deciding whether to roll back. Our release tool also batched every deploy from the week into one Friday train, and the on-call engineer could not tell which change had broken production. The batching made rollbacks slower.

So in March we froze deploys after noon on Friday. In the retro, Ana put it plainly: "I would rather ship on Monday than debug on Sunday." Nobody argued.

Incidents dropped a lot after the freeze. Weekends got quieter, and the Monday queue got longer, which we expected.

The freeze has a cost. A fix that is ready at two on Friday waits until Monday morning, and some weeks that delay annoys a customer. We decided that cost is smaller than a weekend spent reading someone else's code.

The draft is in good shape. Deirdre found no heading-echoes, no three-beat runs, and no closing flourish. Most sentences passed. I made no edits.

## Structural

1. **The result has no number.** "Incidents dropped a lot after the freeze." This sentence is the evidence for the argument, and it is the vaguest sentence in the post. Fact needed from the writer: how many incidents occurred before and after the March freeze, and over what period?

2. **The batching point does not agree with the rest of the post.** Paragraph 1 says "our team shipped whenever a change was ready". Paragraph 2 says "Our release tool also batched every deploy from the week into one Friday train". A reader cannot tell which is true. Batching is also a second cause that a Friday freeze does not clearly fix. Fact needed from the writer: did the team ship each change when it was ready, or one time each week? If the batching was real, what happened to it after the freeze?

## Line notes

- **"The pattern was hard to miss once we read the incident log."** It mostly repeats the sentence before it. The only new fact is the source. Fold the source into the sentence before it, for example "Most of our worst outages in the incident log started on a Friday."
- **"The batching made rollbacks slower."** The sentence before it already shows why. This is a safe cut if note 2 leaves the batching in the post.
- **"some weeks that delay annoys a customer"** This is soft. Fact needed from the writer: how often does this happen, or what is one real case?

## Keep as they are

- Ana's quote and "Nobody argued." The two passes disagreed on "Nobody argued." I recommend that you keep it, because it finishes the paragraph and states a fact.
- "When something breaks at nine on Saturday, the on-call engineer has to read an unfamiliar diff before deciding whether to roll back." This sentence shows the cause as a scene.
- The last paragraph. It names the cost and makes the decision.
